title: Finding text in street photos by letting the network weigh its own shortcuts
paper_title: Multi scale mirror connection based encoder decoder network for text localization
date_note: Accepted 5 April 2020 (Elsevier author manuscript), online in April 2020 with DOI patrec.2020.04.002; exact online day not shown in the PDF, 20 April is a plausible pick.
authors: K Dutta, M Bal, A Basak, Swarnendu Ghosh, N Das, M Kundu, M Nasipuri
summary: A segmentation network that marks which pixels of a street photo are text. Weighted shortcuts between its layers and a vote across three window sizes beat SegNet, U-Net and PSPNet on four public datasets.

body.p: Before a computer can read a shop sign in a photo, it has to find the sign. This paper is about that first step, called text localization. We built a neural network that labels every pixel of an image as text or not text, and we changed the way its layers pass information to each other. On four public datasets it beat three well-known segmentation networks.

Text in the wild is awkward. Lighting is uncontrolled, backgrounds are cluttered, and many ordinary objects happen to look like letters. Text also comes in every size, from a word that fills the frame to a few pixels in a corner, and it can be tilted or curved.

Popular object detectors draw boxes. They start from a set of preset box shapes, called anchor boxes, which are chosen by clustering the boxes in the training data. Text boxes vary so much in size and aspect ratio that a fixed set of shapes fits them badly. Since text finding only needs a yes or no answer, we dropped boxes altogether. The network outputs a mask, a black and white picture the size of the input, where white pixels are text. This is binary segmentation, and it handles curved text without extra effort.

We used an encoder-decoder network. The encoder squeezes the image through a series of layers, each giving a coarser summary. The decoder then expands that summary back into a full-size mask. Squeezing throws away fine detail, so a network called U-Net adds skip connections: shortcuts that copy features from an encoder layer straight across to the matching decoder layer.

A plain shortcut has a weakness. Every bridge feeds the decoder with the same weight and nobody controls the total flow, so one layer can drown out the others. We replaced the bridges with three kinds of mirror connection:

ul: Linear. Add the encoder features to the decoder as they are, as U-Net does.
Parametric. Multiply the encoder features by one trainable number first, so the network learns how loudly each bridge should speak.
Convolutional. Pass the features through an extra small encoder and decoder pair before adding them. This gives finer control but needs more memory.

body.p: Inside each layer we also added internal skips, in the style of residual networks, so that the learning signal reaches the early layers more easily.

figure.alt: Diagram of an encoder-decoder network with coloured blocks shrinking and then growing again. Boxes labelled Mirror Skip link each encoder layer to its mirror layer in the decoder, and small loops mark internal skips. A street-sign photo goes in and a black and white mask comes out.
figure.caption: The base network. The long arcs labelled Mirror Skip are the connections we studied, and the short loops are the internal skips.

body.h2: Three window sizes and a vote

body.p: A convolution looks at the image through a small sliding window, called a kernel. A small window sees fine strokes and a larger one sees more context. For each type of mirror connection we trained three networks with 3×3, 5×5 and 7×7 windows, so nine in total. To get the final mask we kept a pixel as text only where the three networks agreed, which removes many false alarms.

figure.alt: Three encoder-decoder networks labelled 3x3, 5x5 and 7x7 kernel each produce an output; a large arrow merges the three outputs by a logical and into the final output.
figure.caption: The three networks with different kernel sizes are merged with a logical and.

body.p: We tested on ICDAR 2003, SVT, ICDAR 2015 and Total-Text. The first three label text with rectangles. Total-Text contains curved text. We held back roughly 20% of the training data for tuning. We report the F-score, one number between 0 and 1 that mixes precision (how much of the marked text is real) with recall (how much of the real text was found).

Single networks were uneven. On SVT, for example, individual F-scores ranged from 0.57 to 0.74, and no kernel size or connection type won everywhere. The pattern only showed once we merged the three window sizes. The parametric version then gave the best F-score on SVT (0.84), ICDAR 2003 (0.87) and ICDAR 2015 (0.79). The linear U-Net-style connection came behind it on all four datasets.

body.callout: On curved text (Total-Text) the merged models scored F-scores of 0.89 (parametric) and 0.90 (convolutional). SegNet, U-Net and PSPNet scored 0.71, 0.75 and 0.75.

body.p: The convolutional connection came out slightly ahead only on Total-Text, which suggests that curved masks profit from its finer control. The sample masks agree with the numbers. Parametric networks drew cleaner shapes and showed less uncertainty in their soft masks, the raw probabilities before we threshold them at 0.5.

figure.alt: A grid of four street-scene photos at the top with curved text on signs, and below them the ground truth mask followed by soft and hard masks from the linear, parametric and convolutional models and from PSPNet, SegNet and U-Net.
figure.caption: Total-Text samples, one column per photo. The hard masks from our models follow the curved text, while the SegNet and U-Net rows at the bottom often miss it or break it up.

body.p: The convolutional connection costs more memory, and we note that it can over-fit the training data. The datasets are small, with 100 to 1,255 training images, so the margins should be read with that in mind. The network also only says where text is. It does not read it. The paper points to splitting text into single characters as a natural next step.
Reading shop names and road signs can help a navigation system, as the paper's introduction points out, and none of that starts until the text has been found.
